technical.prompt: What is a structured note?
expectedPoints: A debt security whose return is linked to an underlying asset

choices.answer: A debt security combining a bond with derivatives to link returns to an asset
distractors: A share issued by a derivatives exchange
A government bond with a fixed coupon only
A loan that pays no interest at all

technical.prompt: How is a capital-protected note typically built?
expectedPoints: A zero-coupon bond that returns the principal
Remaining money buys options for upside
Principal protection depends on issuer credit
Participation depends on rates and option prices

choices.answer: A zero-coupon bond for protection plus options for upside
distractors: Only stocks bought with borrowed money
Only put options on a stock index
Only cash held in a savings account

technical.prompt: What is a reverse convertible?
expectedPoints: Investor may receive shares instead of principal if the stock falls
Investor has effectively sold a put

choices.answer: A high-coupon note that may repay in shares if the stock falls
distractors: A bond that converts into cash if the stock rises
A note paying a coupon only when the stock rises
A share that turns into a bond at maturity

technical.prompt: What is an autocallable note?
expectedPoints: Redeems early if the underlying is above a level on observation dates
Pays a coupon on early redemption
Downside risk if a barrier is breached

choices.answer: A note that redeems early with a coupon if the underlying is above a set level
distractors: A note automatically sold every day at noon
A note that can only be redeemed at final maturity
A note that pays out only if markets crash

technical.prompt: What is a barrier option?
expectedPoints: An option that activates or cancels if the price hits a level
Hedging is harder near the barrier

choices.answer: An option that switches on or off if the price hits a set level
distractors: An option that can't be traded across borders
An option limited to one trader
An option with a fixed price that never changes

technical.prompt: What is a digital option?
expectedPoints: Pays a fixed amount if a condition is met
Hedging is hard near the strike at expiry

choices.answer: An option paying a fixed amount if a condition is met, otherwise nothing
distractors: An option traded only on electronic exchanges
An option whose payoff grows without limit
An option on a technology company

technical.prompt: What is a variance swap?
expectedPoints: Pays the difference between realised and agreed variance
Used to trade or hedge volatility

choices.answer: A swap paying the difference between realised and agreed variance
distractors: A swap exchanging two different currencies
A swap paying the difference between two stock prices
A swap exchanging fixed and floating interest

technical.prompt: Why does the issuer's credit risk matter to structured note investors?
expectedPoints: Notes are unsecured debt of the issuer
If the issuer defaults, investors can lose principal

choices.answer: Notes are unsecured debt, so an issuer default can cost investors principal
distractors: The underlying asset guarantees repayment
Structured notes are insured by governments
Issuer risk only affects the coupon

technical.prompt: Who buys structured products?

choices.answer: Retail and private bank clients, institutions, insurers and corporates
distractors: Only central banks managing foreign reserves
Only the issuing bank's own trading desks
Only the exchanges that list the products

technical.prompt: What is a participation rate?
expectedPoints: Share of the underlying's gain the investor receives
Can exceed 100% with caps or other features

choices.answer: The share of the underlying's gain paid to the investor
distractors: The percentage of investors who buy the note
The interest rate on the zero-coupon bond
The fee paid to the distributor

technical.prompt: What is a knock-in put?
expectedPoints: A put that only becomes active if the price falls to a barrier
Common in autocallables and reverse convertibles

choices.answer: A put that becomes active only if the price falls to a barrier
distractors: A put that disappears if the price falls
A put paying out only when prices rise
A put on a bond instead of a stock

technical.prompt: How do banks earn money on structured products?
expectedPoints: Margin between price and fair value

choices.answer: Margin over fair value, hedging and funding benefits
distractors: Structured products earn banks nothing
Banks earn only from investor losses
Governments pay banks to issue them

technical.prompt: What is a worst-of structure?
expectedPoints: Payoff depends on the worst-performing of several assets

choices.answer: A payoff linked to the worst-performing of several assets
distractors: A payoff linked to the best performer
A product that averages all assets
A product rated worst by agencies

technical.prompt: How does a dealer hedge the options embedded in structured products?

choices.answer: By delta hedging and managing volatility with listed options
distractors: It never hedges and hopes for the best
It sells the notes to another bank
Structured products need no hedging

technical.prompt: Why do regulators focus on structured products sold to retail investors?

choices.answer: They are complex and may hide risks and fees from retail investors
distractors: Retail investors can't lose money
Structured products are always simple
Regulators don't care about retail

technical.prompt: Why do structured products often leave banks short volatility or long volatility in aggregate?
expectedPoints: Investors often sell options embedded in notes
Banks end up long volatility from high-coupon notes

choices.answer: Investors often sell embedded options, leaving banks long volatility overall
distractors: Banks never hold any volatility exposure
Investors always buy volatility from banks
Volatility exposure disappears at issuance

technical.prompt: What affects the price of a capital-protected note?

choices.answer: Rates, option costs, issuer spread, dividends and fees
distractors: Only the design of the note's printed term sheet
Only the age of the investor buying the note
Only the day of the week on which it is sold

technical.prompt: What is correlation risk in multi-asset products?
expectedPoints: Value depends on how assets move together

choices.answer: Value depends on how the assets move together, which is hard to hedge
distractors: The risk that two traders on a desk disagree
The risk that prices don't respond to news
The risk that two stock indices merge

technical.prompt: Why are exotic options harder to hedge than plain options?

choices.answer: Path-dependence, jumpy payoffs and model risk complicate hedging
distractors: Exotic options never change in price
Exotic options are always exchange-traded
Exotic options have no Greeks to manage

technical.prompt: A 5-year capital-protected note on 100 invests in a zero-coupon bond yielding 4%. At-the-money 5-year calls cost 25 per 100. What participation rate can it offer?

choices.answer: About 71%
distractors: About 82%
About 18%

choices.answer: 80, a 20% loss
distractors: 110, a 10% gain
100, breakeven

technical.prompt: A note sells at 100 but its fair value is 97. What does that mean?
expectedPoints: About 3% of value retained as margin and costs

choices.answer: About 3% is retained by the issuer and distributors
distractors: The investor gains 3% immediately

technical.prompt: Why do capital-protected notes offer better participation when interest rates are high?

choices.answer: The zero-coupon bond costs less, leaving more to buy options
distractors: High rates make options cheaper to buy
High rates reduce the issuer's credit risk

technical.prompt: Why can reverse convertibles offer high coupons?
expectedPoints: Investor sells a put on the stock

choices.answer: The investor effectively sells a put whose premium funds the coupon
distractors: The issuer guarantees the stock's future price
The coupon is paid entirely from dividends
A high coupon means the note carries no risk

technical.prompt: Why can hedging a barrier option be difficult near the barrier?
expectedPoints: Small moves can switch the option on or off

choices.answer: Small moves can switch it on or off, so the Greeks jump
distractors: Barrier options have no Greeks to hedge
Hedging gets easier as the barrier nears
Barrier levels are never actually reached

technical.prompt: Why do worst-of products pay higher coupons than single-asset products?
expectedPoints: Probability of at least one asset falling is higher

choices.answer: The chance of at least one asset falling is higher
distractors: They always have less risk
They are guaranteed by governments
Higher correlation increases coupons

technical.prompt: Why might an investor buy a variance swap rather than options to trade volatility?
expectedPoints: Payoff independent of price path direction

choices.answer: It gives pure volatility exposure without delta hedging
distractors: Variance swaps have no risk
Options can't trade volatility
Variance swaps pay dividends

technical.prompt: How would you check whether a structured note suits a retail client?

choices.answer: Check risk tolerance, understanding, horizon, liquidity and concentration
distractors: Sell it if the client has enough cash
Check only whether the client likes the coupon
Suitability checks aren't needed for notes

technical.prompt: Why do dealers selling many autocallables become exposed to volatility and skew?

distractors: Credit spread doesn't affect notes

technical.prompt: What happens to an autocallable if markets fall and the knock-in barrier is breached?

choices.answer: The investor takes losses at maturity much like owning the stock
distractors: The investor is repaid in full regardless

technical.prompt: What disclosures should accompany a structured product?

choices.answer: Risks, fees and fair value, scenarios, issuer credit and liquidity
distractors: Only the product's marketing name
Only the expected best-case return
No disclosures are needed for notes

technical.prompt: What is a cliquet option?

choices.answer: A series of forward-starting options that lock in periodic gains
distractors: An option that pays only once at the start
An option on a single day's close
An option that can be sold only to clubs

technical.prompt: What is model risk in structured products?

distractors: The risk of a fashion model endorsing a product
